        Whitespace padding in filenames bypasses file upload extension checks

Description

  

    
Impact

A bypass was identified in OWASP CRS that allows uploading files with dangerous extensions (.php, .phar, .jsp, .jspx) by inserting whitespace padding in the filename (e.g. photo. php or shell.jsp ). The affected rules do not normalize whitespace before evaluating the file extension regex, so the dot-extension check fails to match.

This affects:

rule 933110 (PHP Script File Upload Found) — PL1

rule 933111 (PHP Double-Extension File Upload) — PL3

rule 944140 (JSP File Upload Detection) — PL1

All paranoia levels up to and including PL4 are affected. If the backend normalizes or strips whitespace from filenames (common on Windows), an attacker can execute arbitrary code by uploading web shells disguised with whitespace-padded extensions.

Users running CRS versions prior to the fix with applications that handle file uploads are impacted.

Patches

The problem has been patched by adding t:removeWhitespace transformation to the affected rules, ensuring filenames are normalized before extension checks:

#4546 — fix for rule 933110

#4547 — fix for rule 933111

#4548 — fix for rule 944140

#4549 — fix for rule 932180

👉  Users should upgrade to the next CRS release containing these fixes.

Workarounds

enforce filename validation at the application level: reject uploads with whitespace in or around file extensions

store uploaded files outside the webroot and rename them to random, safe filenames

configure the web server to never execute uploaded files regardless of extension

add a custom rule to strip whitespace from FILES and FILES_NAMES variables before processing, e.g. by adding t:removeWhitespace to local copies of rules 933110, 933111, and 944140

References

reported by @HackingRepo as KP3-260311 on 2026-03-10

PR #4546 — fix(933110)

PR #4547 — fix(933111)

PR #4548 — fix(944140)

PR #4549 — fix(932180)

PR #4581 - fix v3

Why Medium

The bypass requires a Windows backend that normalizes whitespace in filenames before executing them; on Linux, files with whitespace-padded extensions (e.g. . php) are not interpreted as executable, making practical exploitation environment-dependent and raising attack complexity.
